title: India's Factory Engine Just Hit Its Second-Lowest Gear in Four Years
excerpt: June manufacturing PMI slipped to 54.2 as cooling demand and Europe's shrinking appetite for Indian goods dragged on output, hiring and business confidence.
body:
India's manufacturing sector, long the workhorse of the economy's post-pandemic recovery, expanded at its second-slowest pace in four years in June, raising fresh questions about the durability of the industrial boom that has powered record capital spending and a swelling stock market.

The HSBC India Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index, compiled by S&P Global, fell to 54.2 in June from 55.0 in May — slightly below the preliminary flash estimate of 54.5. Only March 2026's reading was weaker going back to mid-2022. Despite the slip, the index remained above the 50.0 threshold that separates expansion from contraction, and sat in line with the long-run series average.

## Demand Is Cooling — Especially From Europe

The softening is being led by orders. New orders — the most closely watched leading indicator in the PMI basket — rose at their second-weakest rate since June 2022, a sharp reversal from the three-month high hit in May. International demand was notably weaker: export orders grew at the slowest pace in 39 months, with firms singling out subdued demand from European clients.

The European drag matters for India's manufacturing complex, which has spent three years pivoting toward diversified export markets as Western companies reconfigure supply chains away from China. If Europe is pulling back, the substitution story loses a critical market.

Capital goods production, a proxy for business investment, was a particular weak spot, dragging overall output growth to its second-lowest reading since mid-2022.

## Prices Are Easing, But That Is a Double-Edged Sword

There is a silver lining for policymakers: cost pressures are retreating. Input cost inflation eased to a four-month low, though firms continued to flag rising prices for chemicals, metals, petroleum products and plastics. Output charges rose at the slowest rate in three months, with 93 per cent of companies leaving prices unchanged from May.

For the Reserve Bank of India, which cut rates in April and has signalled openness to further easing, the cooling price picture strengthens the case for another move as early as August. But the RBI will also be watching for signs that softening demand is becoming self-reinforcing — weaker orders leading to weaker hiring leading to weaker consumption.

## Hiring Has Stalled

That feedback loop may already be forming. Employment grew at its weakest pace this year, with 97 per cent of firms keeping headcount unchanged, citing adequate existing capacity. Business confidence dropped to a five-month low as firms expressed growing concern about demand conditions and market uncertainty.

## What It Means for the Bigger Picture

India's manufacturing PMI remains one of the strongest in the world. A June survey of 18 countries showed the global median PMI at just 47.8, meaning most major economies are seeing outright contraction. India's 54.2 puts it in the 92nd percentile historically — comfortably in expansion territory and well ahead of peers like Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.

But the trajectory matters more than the level. Three months ago, India's PMI sat near 57; now it has slipped to the low 54s. If this is a soft patch driven by temporary European demand wobbles and the tail end of the oil shock, the recovery could be swift. If it reflects a structural cooling as India's post-pandemic catch-up spending fades, the government's infrastructure-led growth strategy faces a harder test.

## The Diaspora Angle

For NRIs with exposure to Indian equities, the PMI data is a reminder that the market's 25 per cent rally over the past quarter was built partly on expectations of accelerating industrial growth. A sustained manufacturing slowdown could test those valuations, particularly in capital goods and mid-cap industrial stocks.

For Indian tech professionals in the US, UK and Canada working in supply chain and manufacturing technology, the signal is nuanced: India's factory floor is slowing but still growing faster than almost anywhere else — the opportunity to build for Indian manufacturing has not gone away, even if the urgency has dimmed.
